unit.title: Perform manual metal arc welding process to AWS specification (Alloy steel pipe)

summary: This unit is about welding low-alloy chromium-molybdenum (Cr-Mo) steel pipe with manual metal arc welding (MMAW) to an AWS specification and a welding procedure specification (WPS). You will learn why alloy pipe cracks more easily than carbon steel, and how matching low-hydrogen electrodes, preheat, interpass control and heat treatment after welding prevent it. You will also learn to identify the material, fit up and weld the joint in fixed positions, inspect and test it, repair it to procedure and keep the records a client expects.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers MMAW of **alloy steel pipe**, mainly the low-alloy **chromium-molybdenum (Cr-Mo)** steels used for steam and hot lines in boilers, power stations, sugar factories, food plants and refineries. The work is done **to AWS specification**: to the AWS code the Centre uses, through a WPS and the records that prove the weld was made as the WPS says.

Alloy pipe is welded with the same basic skills as carbon steel pipe, but with much tighter control. A Cr-Mo weld that is made with damp electrodes, without preheat, or cooled too fast can look perfect and then crack hours later. Most of this unit is about the controls that stop that happening, and about showing on paper that they were applied.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees who can already weld carbon steel pipe with MMAW, and who will now plan, weld, check and record alloy pipe work, often as the leader of a small team.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work to the specification and the WPS
Read the WPS, the weld map and the inspection plan; follow every variable and hold point; never change a variable without approval.
Check pipe and electrodes against the drawing, mill certificates and WPS; keep alloy grades apart and traceable.
Keep matching alloy electrodes in ovens and quivers, re-dry or scrap them as the maker says, and record batches.
Heat the joint evenly, measure the temperature correctly and keep it within the WPS range from tacking to the last pass.
Prepare and fit up the joint
Cut, bevel, clean and line up the pipe; set the root face, gap and alignment; tack with preheat.
Weld 5G and 6G joints uphill with low-hydrogen electrodes, from the root to the cap.
Understand heat treatment after welding, visual inspection, NDT, hardness and bend tests, and repair a rejected weld to procedure.
Work safely and lead the team
Control burns, fume, gas, electrical and heat-stress hazards; plan the work; keep the weld, heat and inspection records.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on specifications, electrodes, alloy steel, preheat and interpass, heat treatment, preparation, technique, defects, inspection and testing, qualification, safety, records and calculations.
A **written paper** with short answers and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practicals**: planning, preheating and welding a low-alloy pipe butt joint in the 5G or 6G position with a heat log; and inspecting and testing pipe coupons with an inspection report.

blocks.note: Many questions ask what you would do as team leader when something goes wrong: a skipped preheat, damp electrodes, an interrupted heat treatment, a failed test. The answer is almost always: stop, follow the WPS or the approved procedure, record it and report it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Alloy steel pipe and why it is harder to weld

blocks.p: Chromium and molybdenum make steel keep its strength at high temperature and resist creep (slow stretching under load) and scaling. That is why these steels carry steam and hot oil. Pipe grades are named in the American standard for alloy pipe by a **P number** after the grade, such as P11 or P22.

head: Pipe grade (typical)
Main alloy
Typical use
Usual matching MMAW electrode
rows: Steam lines and headers, boiler pipework
Higher-alloy electrodes, as the WPS names
Special electrodes and very strict control; beyond this unit

blocks.note: The filler must **match** the pipe's alloy, so the weld has the same strength and heat resistance as the pipe. An E8018-B2 weld on P22, or a carbon steel E7018 weld on P11, can fail in service even if it passes every test on the day.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Chromium and molybdenum make steel **harden easily**. When the weld cools quickly, the parent metal next to it, the **heat-affected zone (HAZ)**, can turn hard and brittle. A hard zone is easily cracked by hydrogen.
**Hydrogen cracking** (also called cold cracking or delayed cracking) needs three things at the same time:

ul: **Hydrogen** in the weld, from moisture in electrode coatings, damp or dirty joints, rust, oil, paint or rain.
A **hard, crack-sensitive structure**, from a hardenable steel cooling fast.
**Stress**, from the weld shrinking against restraint.

blocks.p: The cracks form as the weld cools to near room temperature, often **hours or even a day or two later**, usually in the HAZ under or beside the weld. They are often too fine to see. Remove any one of the three causes and the cracking stops. The WPS attacks all three.

head: Control in the WPS
What it does
rows: Removes rust, oil, paint and water, which all bring hydrogen
Slows cooling, so less hard zone forms, and gives hydrogen time to escape
Stops the joint overheating, which would spoil the weld's toughness and strength
Slow cooling, or post-heat, after welding
Lets more hydrogen escape before the joint gets cold
Tempers (softens and toughens) the hard zone and relieves locked-in stress
A good fit-up and welding sequence

blocks.p: Carbon steel and Cr-Mo pipe look the same. A wrong piece in a hot steam line can fail and kill. So material control is strict:

ul: Each pipe carries its grade, size, schedule and **heat number**. Check the heat number against the **mill certificate**, which gives its chemical analysis and test results, and against the drawing.
Keep alloy pipe, fittings and electrodes apart from carbon steel and from other grades. Many yards paint a colour band on each grade; follow the yard's colour code.
Before a length is cut, **transfer the heat number and grade** onto every piece that will be cut from it, so each offcut stays traceable.

Material with no markings, or markings that do not match a certificate, is **quarantined**, not used. It may be identified by **positive material identification (PMI)**: a hand-held analyser that reads the alloy content.
Record the heat numbers on the weld map or weld log, so every piece in the line can be traced.

sections.title: Specifications, procedures, records and leading the team

blocks.p: "To AWS specification" means the work must meet the rules of the AWS code or standard the client names, through procedures and welders qualified to it. It does not mean American pipe or American-trained welders; it means following the rules and being able to prove it.

head: Document
What it is for
rows: Show the line and give every weld its own number
The method for each joint: pipe grade and thickness range, joint design, electrodes, current, positions, preheat, interpass, post-heat and PWHT
The record that the WPS was tested and passed: the real values used and the test results
Each welder's test record: the process, positions, sizes and electrode groups the welder may weld
The checks at each stage, with **hold points** where work stops until the inspector has seen it
Prove the pipe grade and the electrode batch
Record, for each weld: welder, electrode batch, preheat and interpass readings, times
The recorder's chart of temperature against time for each heat treatment
The results of every test, with the weld number

blocks.p: Every weld can then be traced: who welded it, with which electrode batch, at what temperatures, how it was heat treated and how it was tested. If a weld fails in service, the records show what went wrong.

blocks.note: Records must be true. Writing a preheat that was not reached, or signing a chart that was not checked, is falsifying a record. It can put lives at risk, and it ends careers.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Read the drawings, specification, WPS and ITP; list the joints on the weld map
Check each welder's WPQ against the positions, sizes and processes, and give out joints to suit
Check pipe, fittings and electrodes against certificates and the WPS; check ovens, quivers, heating equipment and welding sets
Plan the order so each joint can be preheated, welded and kept warm without long breaks, and book the heat treatment
Brief the team at a toolbox talk: the WPS, hold points, burns, fume, heat stress and hot work
During the work: check fit-ups, preheat and interpass readings, electrode handling and each root before the next pass
Stop the work and report anything outside the WPS; never cover it up
Complete and check the records, then report to your supervisor

head: Sum
Example
rows: 6 passes × (10 min arc + 6 min cleaning and checks) = 96 min = **1 h 36 min**, plus preheat time
One pass round NPS 6 pipe: π × 168.3 = **529 mm**; 8 joints × 529 mm ≈ **4.2 m** per pass
If about 60% of the electrode mass ends up in the weld, 0.9 kg of weld needs 0.9 ÷ 0.6 = **1.5 kg** of electrodes
100 mm each side of the joint = **200 mm** wide, plus the weld

blocks.note: If someone in the team skips a preheat "because Jamaica is hot", stop the work. Air at 33 °C is far below a preheat of 150 °C. Preheat the joint to the WPS, find out what was welded without it, report it, and let the engineer decide whether those welds must be cut out or tested.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Safety and health on alloy pipe work

blocks.p: Alloy pipe work adds long periods of hot metal, gas heating torches, electric heating equipment and insulation to the usual arc welding hazards.

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: Burns from preheated and heat-treated pipe (often 150–300 °C for hours, and far hotter during PWHT)
Mark the pipe HOT and put up barriers
Never touch pipe or heating pads to test the heat
Hoses and fittings checked; flashback arrestors fitted
Keep the flame moving and away from hoses and anything that burns
Cylinders upright and secured, away from the heat
Electric heating pads and power units
Set up and run only by a trained, authorised heat-treatment operator
Cables checked and kept dry; units earthed as the maker says
Keep out of the heated area
Gloves, long sleeves and a dust mask when handling
Bag up old blankets; do not shake them out
Local extraction close to the arc
Respirator where extraction is not enough
Head out of the plume, especially when the hot pipe makes the fume rise fast
Helmet with the right shade; skin covered
Dry PPE; cables and holder checked
Stop or shelter the joint in rain
Team lifts or lifting gear for pipe and fittings
Water, shade and planned rest breaks
Rotate welders on long preheated joints
Watch each other for warning signs

blocks.note: Welding a preheated joint in Jamaica's heat, in full leathers, is hard on the body. Know the signs. **Heat exhaustion**: heavy sweating, weakness, headache, nausea; move to shade, cool down and drink. **Heat stroke**: confusion, collapse, hot skin, sweating may stop; this is an emergency: call for help (110 for an ambulance), cool the person with water and moving air, and stay with them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Never cool a hot Cr-Mo joint with water to make it safe to touch. Fast cooling hardens it and can crack it. Mark it HOT and keep people away.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Low-alloy electrodes are classified like carbon steel electrodes, with a **suffix** that gives the alloy content of the weld metal.

head: Part of E8018-B2
What it tells you
rows: Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal: about 80 000 psi (about 550 MPa)
Low-hydrogen coating with iron powder; AC or DC electrode positive
Weld metal alloy: chromium-molybdenum (about 1¼% Cr, ½% Mo), matching P11

blocks.p: Other suffixes you will meet: **A1** (carbon-molybdenum), **B3** (2¼% Cr-1% Mo, matching P22, usually in E9018-B3), and "L" versions (B2L, B3L) with lower carbon, used only where the WPS names them.

blocks.note: **Never use cellulosic electrodes (E6010, E6011) on Cr-Mo pipe**, not even for the root. Their coating puts a lot of hydrogen into the weld, the very thing that cracks a hard HAZ.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Stage
What to do
rows: Keep in sealed tins in a dry store, labelled by class
Put straight into a **holding oven** at the maker's temperature (often about 120–150 °C). Check the oven is on and at temperature at the start of every shift
A few at a time in a **heated quiver**, lid closed, plugged in

Codes limit time out of the oven; often about 2 hours for E80XX and about 1 hour for E90XX electrodes. Past the limit: return them for **re-drying** exactly as the maker says (often about 350–400 °C for about an hour), only as many times as the maker allows, or scrap them
Cracked or chipped flux, or wet electrodes: scrap them
Write the class and **batch number** on the weld log

ul: Keep each alloy grade in its own labelled oven or compartment, and never let an E7018 (carbon steel) or a different alloy get into a Cr-Mo welder's quiver.
If a wrong electrode is found in use, stop the welder, find out which welds may have been made with it, and report it. Those welds may have to be cut out.

blocks.p: E8018-B2 and E9018-B3 are normally run on **DC electrode positive (DCEP)**. Typical currents:

head: Size
Typical current (follow the WPS and the packet)

blocks.p: Only part of an electrode's mass ends up as weld metal: the stub and the coating do not. If about **60%** becomes weld metal, then electrodes needed = weld metal needed ÷ 0.6. For 1.5 kg of weld metal: 1.5 ÷ 0.6 = 2.5 kg of electrodes. Order a little more for scrapped and re-dried electrodes.

**Preheat** is heating the parent metal to a set temperature before welding (and before tacking). **Interpass temperature** is the temperature of the joint just before each new pass. The WPS gives a **minimum** preheat and a **maximum** interpass; the joint must stay inside that range from the first tack to the last pass.

blocks.note: These are typical figures only. The WPS figures are the ones that count, and they depend on the grade, the wall thickness and the code.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Too much heat, built up by welding pass after pass without waiting, makes the weld and HAZ coarse-grained, lowers the toughness and strength, and can change the heat treatment result. If the joint is above the maximum, **wait** for it to cool in still air. Never cool it with water, a wet rag or compressed air.

head: Method
Points to know
rows: Gas heating torch (propane or other fuel gas)
Simple and portable. Keep the flame moving round the whole band; never hold it on one spot. Hard to keep even on thick pipe
Even, controlled heat with thermocouples and a control unit; can also hold preheat for hours and do PWHT. Run by a trained operator
A coil round the pipe heats it quickly and evenly; also run by trained operators

blocks.p: Heat a **band** all round the joint, as wide as the WPS says (for example 100 mm each side), so the whole thickness is at temperature, not just the surface.

head: Tool
How it works
Watch out
rows: Melts when the metal is at or above its rated temperature; stays a dry, chalky mark below it
Mark on the parent metal, not in the groove. Use two: one at the minimum preheat (must melt) and one at the maximum interpass (must not melt)
A probe pressed on the metal gives a reading
Must be calibrated; hold it until the reading settles
Reads heat radiated from the surface
Must be calibrated and set for the surface; **bright, shiny metal reads low**, so it is unreliable on freshly ground bevels

ul: Measure on the **parent metal at the distance from the joint that the WPS gives**, and on several points round the pipe.

With a torch, take the flame away and wait a short time for the heat to even out through the wall before measuring, or measure on the side away from the flame. A surface reading straight after the flame reads too high.
Check the interpass temperature **before every pass**: above the minimum and below the maximum.
Record each reading on the **heat log**: date, time, weld number, where measured, method, reading and your name.

blocks.p: If heat treatment cannot follow straight away, the WPS will say what to do. Common instructions: keep the joint at preheat until PWHT; or raise it to a higher **post-heat** temperature for a set time to drive hydrogen out; or wrap it in dry insulation so it cools **slowly**. Never leave a Cr-Mo joint to cool fast in a breeze or rain.

blocks.note: Rain on a hot joint cools it fast and brings hydrogen. Stop welding in rain, or shelter the joint completely and keep it dry and at temperature. Do not "weld faster before the rain gets in".
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Preparing and fitting up alloy pipe

flow: Check the pipe grade, size, schedule and heat number against the drawing and mill certificate; transfer the markings before cutting
Cut square by saw or machine where possible. If the pipe is torch cut, preheat it first as for welding, then grind the cut surface back to sound, bright metal
Bevel to the WPS angle (often 37.5° each side, 75° included) and grind the root face to size (often about 1–2 mm)
Clean the bevels and about 25 mm inside and outside to bright metal, removing all rust, scale, oil, paint and marker
Check the bevel angle and root face with a gauge
Set the pipes in a line-up clamp with spacers for the root gap the WPS gives; check alignment all round with a **hi-lo gauge**, within the limit
Preheat to the WPS minimum **before tacking**
Tack with the WPS electrode: small, sound tacks spaced round the pipe, ends ground to a taper
Record the fit-up checks; call the inspector if the ITP has a fit-up hold point

head: Fit-up feature
Why it matters on alloy pipe
rows: Controls how the root melts through: too thick gives lack of penetration, too thin gives burn-through
Too small: lack of penetration. Too wide: burn-through and a hot, slow root
A step inside the bore leaves an unfused root face and a notch that raises stress in a hot, pressurised line
Rust, oil, paint and moisture all bring hydrogen into the weld

blocks.note: Tacks on Cr-Mo crack just as easily as welds. A tack made without preheat can crack before the root reaches it. Tacks are part of the weld: preheat, low-hydrogen electrodes and good fusion apply to them too.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An arc struck on the pipe outside the groove melts a tiny spot that cools almost instantly. On Cr-Mo it forms a **hard spot** that can crack. Strike only in the groove. If an arc strike happens, report it: it is usually ground out smoothly and checked by magnetic particle or dye penetrant testing, as the procedure says.

head: Pass
Points for alloy pipe
rows: Low-hydrogen electrode (often 2.5 mm) or, where the WPS says, a GTAW root with matching wire. Short arc; keep a small keyhole
Straight after the root has been cleaned, to burn out slag lines along its edges and thicken it
Stringers or a limited weave, as the WPS allows; clean and check interpass temperature before each pass
Even weave just past the bevel edges, no undercut, height within the code limit

flow: Check the preheat all round the joint
Start the root just past 6 o'clock, striking in the groove
Weld uphill to just past 12 o'clock on one side, keeping a short arc and changing the electrode angle as you go round
Grind the start and stop of the first half to a taper
Weld the second half from the bottom, tying into the tapered start, and over the top into the tapered stop
Clean the root fully, grind any high spots, check the interpass temperature, then run the hot pass
Fill and cap the same way, staggering starts and stops round the pipe

blocks.p: **6G** (pipe fixed at 45°) is welded the same way, uphill from the bottom in two halves, but the joint also slopes, so the electrode angle must change in two directions as you go round.

ul: **Short arc** at all times, about the core wire diameter or less. A long arc breaks the gas shield and lets air in: porosity and nitrogen in the weld.
Do **not** whip the electrode out of the pool as you would with E6010. Keep the arc in the pool and control the keyhole with travel speed, a slight side-to-side movement and the angle.
Strike **just ahead** of where the pass starts, in the groove, then move back over the start point. This melts out the porosity a cold start can leave.
Keep the weave within the width the WPS allows. A wide weave puts in more heat and lets the shield cool and thin at the edges.
Grind starts and stops to a taper before tying in, so craters and cold laps do not stay in the joint.
Clean each pass with a power wire brush; grind out any slag, porosity or bad stop before the next pass.

blocks.note: Low-hydrogen fill and cap give stronger, tougher weld metal, but they are less forgiving than cellulosic electrodes. Most faults on alloy pipe roots come from a long arc, a poor tie-in or a cold start.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A Cr-Mo joint should be welded without long breaks. If the work must stop (end of shift, rain, a fault), follow the WPS: often the joint must be filled to a minimum depth first, then kept at preheat or post-heated and wrapped in dry insulation to cool slowly. Before welding starts again, preheat it back to the WPS minimum and record it.

ul: A welder's WPQ covers the process tested: an MMAW test does not cover a GTAW root. If the WPS calls for a GTAW root and MMAW fill, each part is welded by someone qualified for that process.
A 6G pipe test generally covers all positions, within the code's limits for diameter, thickness and electrode group.
For a 6G bend test, strips are cut from set places round the coupon, so the overhead, vertical and flat parts of the joint are all tested.

sections.title: Heat treatment, inspection, testing and repairs

blocks.p: PWHT heats the welded joint slowly to a high temperature, holds it there, then cools it slowly. It **tempers** the hard HAZ, making it tougher, **relieves the stresses** locked in by welding, and lets remaining hydrogen escape.

head: The WPS sets
Typical for P11 and P22 (follow the WPS)
rows: Heating rate above a set temperature
Often about 1 hour per 25 mm of wall, with a minimum time
Controlled down to a set temperature, then still air
So the whole joint and the HAZ reach temperature, without sharp temperature changes

ul: PWHT is done by a **trained, authorised operator** with heating pads, induction coils or a furnace.
**Thermocouples** are fixed to the pipe at set places; a **recorder** draws a chart of temperature against time for the whole cycle.
The chart is checked against the WPS limits, signed and filed with the weld records.

If the cycle is interrupted (a power cut, a burnt-out pad) or goes outside the limits, it is **recorded and reported**. The engineer decides what happens next: the cycle may be completed, repeated, or the weld tested further. Nobody quietly restarts it and signs it off.

A **hardness test** on the weld and HAZ after PWHT checks that the treatment worked. A reading above the code's maximum is reported; the joint usually needs further heat treatment as the engineer directs.

blocks.p: Visual inspection comes first, on every weld, in good light, with a weld gauge, mirror and torch.

ul: Check the weld number and welder's mark.
Cap all round: cracks, porosity, undercut deeper than the code allows, overlap, arc strikes, spatter, cap width and height.
Root where it can be seen: full penetration, concavity, excess penetration, burn-through.
Alignment and the heat log: were preheat and interpass inside the WPS range?
Report each fault by **clock position** and size, with a decision: accept, reject or further testing.

head: NDT method
What it finds
Notes on alloy pipe
rows: Buried slag, lack of fusion and penetration, porosity, cracks
The usual volumetric test on pipe butt welds; licensed operators only
Lack of fusion and cracks, especially in thick walls
Cracks at or just below the surface
Cr-Mo is magnetic, so MT works well on caps, repairs and arc strikes
Cracks and pores open to the surface
Whether the HAZ and weld are too hard

blocks.note: Because hydrogen cracks can appear hours after welding, many specifications say final NDT must be done after PWHT, or not until a set time (often 24–48 hours) after welding.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: The coupon is welded to a qualified WPS, with an inspector watching preparation, preheat and welding
Visual inspection of cap and root
Bend strips cut from set places round the coupon (or radiography, where the code allows)
Strips dressed flush, edges rounded, bent in a guided jig
Open defects measured against the code's limit; results recorded on the WPQ and signed

blocks.p: A defect in a Cr-Mo weld is never covered over with another pass, hammered or ground flush to hide it. It is repaired to an **approved repair procedure**:

flow: Mark the defect's position and length from the NDT report
Preheat as the repair procedure says, then remove the defect by grinding (or gouging, then grinding)
Check by MT or PT that it is completely gone; keep grinding until the check is clean
Re-weld with preheat, matching electrodes and interpass control
Post-heat or slow cool, then heat treat again as the procedure says
Repeat the NDT (and hardness test) on the repaired area; record the repair on the weld log

blocks.note: Each repair heats the joint again and adds risk. Many specifications allow only one or two repairs in the same place before the engineer must decide whether to cut the joint out.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what working "to AWS specification" means, and use the WPS, PQR, WPQ, weld map and ITP.
I can name common Cr-Mo pipe grades and their matching electrodes.
I can explain hydrogen cracking: its three causes and how the WPS controls each one.
I can identify alloy pipe from its markings and mill certificate, keep it traceable and quarantine unknown material.
I can read an alloy electrode class such as E8018-B2 and store, issue, re-dry or scrap low-hydrogen electrodes correctly.
I can preheat a joint evenly, measure the temperature correctly and keep it within the interpass range.
I can convert temperatures between °C and °F.
I can prepare, clean, fit up and tack an alloy pipe joint with preheat.
I can weld a 5G or 6G alloy pipe joint uphill with low-hydrogen electrodes.
I can explain the purpose of PWHT, what the WPS sets for it and how it is recorded.
I can inspect an alloy pipe weld, report faults by clock position and say which NDT method finds which fault.
I can describe how a defect is repaired to procedure.
I can control the hazards of preheating, welding and heat treating, including heat stress.
I can plan the work of a small team and keep complete, true records.

terms: Low-alloy steel used for hot and high-pressure lines
Cracking caused by hydrogen in a hard zone under stress, often hours after welding
Low-hydrogen MMAW electrode with 1¼Cr-½Mo weld metal, matching P11 pipe
Record of preheat and interpass readings for each joint
The number linking a pipe to its batch of steel and its mill certificate
The parent metal next to the weld that was changed by the heat but did not melt
A gauge that measures misalignment between pipe walls
A stage where work stops until the inspector has checked it
A heated oven that keeps opened low-hydrogen electrodes dry
The joint temperature just before each pass
An electrode whose coating puts very little hydrogen into the weld
The steel maker's certificate of chemical analysis and test results
Finding surface cracks in steel with a magnet and fine iron powder
Finding surface-breaking flaws with a dye that seeps in and is drawn out
Positive material identification: checking alloy content with an analyser
Holding the joint at a raised temperature after welding to drive out hydrogen
Heating the parent metal to a set temperature before welding
A heated portable container for electrodes on the job
Reheating hard steel to make it tougher and less brittle
A temperature sensor fixed to the pipe during heat treatment
A drawing that shows every weld with its own number

c1.title: A boiler header at a food factory in Montego Bay
c1.text: Nadine leads a team welding a P11 (1¼Cr-½Mo) steam header in NPS 6 schedule 80 pipe at a food factory in Montego Bay, St James. The WPS calls for E8018-B2 electrodes on DCEP, a minimum preheat of 150 °C measured 50 mm from the joint, a maximum interpass of 315 °C, and PWHT. The specification says RT and MT must not be done until 48 hours after welding.

c2.title: Material checks at a contractor's yard in Old Harbour
c2.text: A truck delivers P11 and P22 pipe for two lines to a contractor's yard in Old Harbour, St Catherine. Each length has its grade and heat number stencilled on it. Jermaine, the storeman, finds a 1.2 m offcut of alloy pipe in the rack with no markings, and the fitter must cut one 6 m length of P22 into three spool pieces.

c3.title: A heat-treatment cycle in May Pen
c3.text: An authorised operator is heat treating a welded P11 joint with electric pads at a plant in May Pen, Clarendon. The client's WPS, written in °F, gives a holding temperature of 1 300 °F and a holding time of 1 hour per 25 mm of wall, with a 1-hour minimum. The header wall is 50 mm. Forty minutes into the hold, a power cut stops the heating unit for 25 minutes before the generator is started.

c4.title: A crack repair on a steam line in St Ann's Bay
c4.text: MT on a P11 steam line weld at a plant in St Ann's Bay, St Ann, shows a 20 mm crack along the toe of the cap at 4 o'clock. The engineer issues an approved repair procedure. After the first grinding, Andre checks the area with MT again and the indication is still there, shorter than before.

c5.title: Planning a week of alloy pipe work in Kingston
c5.text: Kerry-Ann, Omar and Delroy will weld P22 joints at a power-plant contractor's shop in Kingston. The WPS calls for a GTAW root with matching wire and E9018-B3 fill and cap. Kerry-Ann holds an MMAW 6G qualification only; Omar holds GTAW and MMAW 6G. The ITP has a hold point before each root is welded. The shop is very hot in the early afternoon.

questions.q: Before tacking, an infrared thermometer pointed at the freshly ground bevel reads 95 °C, but a calibrated contact thermometer on the pipe 50 mm from the joint reads 165 °C. What should Nadine do?
o: Average the two readings to 130 °C and keep heating the joint
Go by the infrared reading, as it was taken where the weld will go
Go by the contact reading at the WPS point; shiny metal fools infrared
Rub a crayon on the bevel inside the groove to settle which one is right
questions.why: Bright, freshly ground metal reflects heat and makes an infrared thermometer read low. The WPS says where to measure: on the parent metal 50 mm from the joint, which the calibrated contact thermometer did.

questions.q: Between passes the joint reads 340 °C. What should the welder do?
o: Wait for it to cool in still air to below 315 °C, then check again
Cool it with a wet rag so the next pass can start without delay
Carry on welding, as extra heat only helps the hydrogen escape
Turn the current down and run the next pass faster to cut the heat
questions.why: The maximum interpass temperature protects the toughness and strength of the weld and HAZ. The joint must cool naturally into the range; water or a wet rag would cool Cr-Mo fast and could harden and crack it.

questions.q: During a check, Nadine finds an E7018 electrode in one welder's quiver among the E8018-B2. What should she do?
o: Remove the E7018 and let him carry on, as the two classes look alike
Stop him, find out which welds may have had E7018, and report it
Let him use it up on the cap only, where the strength matters least
Tell him to re-dry the whole quiver load before he carries on welding
questions.why: E7018 is a carbon steel electrode and does not match P11. Weld metal of the wrong alloy can fail at high temperature, so any weld that may contain it must be identified and reported; it may have to be cut out.

questions.q: Why does the specification make the inspectors wait 48 hours before RT and MT?
o: The weld must cool to air temperature before film can be used
The PWHT chart takes two days to be checked and signed
The magnetic powder sticks only to steel that has fully cooled
Hydrogen cracks can form hours after the weld has cooled
questions.why: Hydrogen (cold) cracks are delayed: they can form many hours after welding. Testing too soon could pass a weld that cracks the next day.

questions.q: What should be done with the unmarked offcut?
o: Use it on the P11 line, since most of the stock is P11
Keep it out of use until its grade is proved and traceable
Paint it with the P22 colour band so the welders know what it is
Use it only for a short pup piece, where the grade matters less
questions.why: Carbon steel, P11 and P22 look the same. Unknown material is quarantined; it may be identified by PMI and matched to a certificate, but it must not be guessed or relabelled.

questions.q: Before the fitter cuts the 6 m length of P22, what must he do?
o: Transfer the grade and heat number onto each piece to be cut
Grind off the stencil marks so they do not get into the weld
Cut it first, then mark the pieces later from the cut list
Ask the mill for a new certificate for each separate piece
questions.why: Once the length is cut, only one piece keeps the original stencil. Marking every piece first keeps each one traceable to its heat number and mill certificate.

questions.q: Which electrode should be issued for MMAW fill and cap passes on the P22 joints?
o: E8018-B2, because it has the higher chromium
E9018-B3, which matches 2¼Cr-1Mo pipe
E7018-A1, as it suits all molybdenum steels
E6010, as long as a hot pass follows
questions.why: P22 is 2¼Cr-1Mo steel and is matched by B3 weld metal, usually E9018-B3. E8018-B2 (1¼Cr-½Mo) matches P11. Cellulosic electrodes are never used on Cr-Mo.

questions.q: What is the WPS holding temperature in °C?
o: About 722 °C
About 690 °C
About 704 °C
About 754 °C
questions.why: °C = (°F − 32) × 5 ÷ 9 = (1 300 − 32) × 5 ÷ 9 = 1 268 × 5 ÷ 9 = 704 °C. Multiplying 1 300 by 5 ÷ 9 without first taking away 32 gives the wrong 722 °C.

questions.q: How long must the joint be held at temperature?
o: 2 hours
1 hour
50 minutes
4 hours
questions.why: 50 mm ÷ 25 mm = 2, so the holding time is 2 hours. The 1-hour minimum applies only to thinner walls, where the sum gives less than an hour.

questions.q: What should happen about the power cut during the hold?
o: Restart the hold from zero quietly and sign the chart as normal
Add 25 minutes to the hold and leave the chart as it is
Raise the temperature 50 °C above the range to make up the time
Record it on the chart and report it, so the engineer decides
questions.why: An interrupted cycle is outside the WPS. The chart shows what happened; the operator records and reports it, and the engineer decides whether to complete, repeat or test further. Nobody adjusts the cycle or the record on their own.

questions.q: After the cycle is complete, a hardness test on the HAZ reads above the code's maximum. What does this most likely mean?
o: The heat treatment did not temper the hard zone enough
The welder used too small an electrode for the cap
The hardness tester must be faulty, as PWHT always works
The pipe was not cleaned to bright metal before welding
questions.why: PWHT tempers the hard HAZ. A reading over the limit shows it has not done its job, often because the temperature or time was short. The result is reported, and the joint usually needs further heat treatment.

questions.q: What should Andre do now?
o: Weld over it, since the crack is now much shorter
Grind it flush so the MT shows nothing, then sign it off
Keep grinding and re-checking until MT shows it is gone
Fill the groove with a cap of E7018, which resists cracking
questions.why: The crack must be removed completely before re-welding, or it will carry on into the new weld. Grind, check with MT, and repeat until the check is clean.

questions.q: The repair has been welded with preheat to the repair procedure. What is still needed before the line goes back into service?
o: Nothing more, as the original weld was already tested
A coat of heat-resistant paint over the repaired area
A visual check by the welder who made the repair
Heat treatment and NDT again, as the procedure says
questions.why: The repair weld has its own hard HAZ and stresses, so it is heat treated again and re-tested (NDT and often hardness) like any new weld, and recorded on the weld log.

questions.q: Which part of the P22 joints may Kerry-Ann weld?
o: Only the MMAW fill and cap; another welder runs the GTAW root
The whole joint, as her 6G test covers every position on pipe
Only the root, as roots are always counted as part of an MMAW test
None of it, until she has passed a separate test on P22 pipe
questions.why: A qualification covers the process tested. Her MMAW 6G test covers MMAW in all positions, but not a GTAW root. Omar, qualified in both processes, can weld the roots.

questions.q: At the hold point before a root, what will the inspector mainly check?
o: The cap width and height, measured all round with a weld gauge
The fit-up, cleanliness, preheat and the materials and electrodes
The PWHT chart and the hardness results recorded for the joint
The radiographs of the root, hot pass and fill from the last joint
questions.why: Before the root, the inspector checks what can only be seen then: bevel, root face, gap, hi-lo and cleanliness, the preheat reading, and that the pipe and filler are the right grade and batch.

questions.q: On a hot afternoon, Delroy becomes confused and unsteady while welding a preheated joint, and his skin is hot. What should the team do first?
o: Give him a cold drink and let him finish the pass first
Send him home to rest and carry on with the work
Call for help, get him into shade and cool him down
Lower the preheat so the joint gives off less heat
questions.why: Confusion and hot skin are signs of heat stroke, an emergency. Call for medical help (110 for an ambulance), move him out of the heat, cool him with water and moving air, and stay with him. The preheat is never lowered for comfort.

questions.q: Hydrogen cracking needs three things at the same time. Which set is it?
o: Hydrogen, a hard crack-sensitive structure, and stress
Hydrogen, a long arc, and a high current
Moisture, a cellulosic electrode, and a cold, damp workshop
A thick wall, a narrow bevel, and a slow travel speed
questions.why: Remove any one of hydrogen, a hard structure or stress and cracking stops. Dry low-hydrogen electrodes and clean joints cut the hydrogen; preheat and PWHT deal with the hard zone; good fit-up and sequence reduce stress.

questions.q: A bevel on a P22 pipe end was cut with an oxy-fuel torch without preheat. What should be done before fit-up?
o: Nothing, as the heat of cutting acts as a preheat
Paint the bevel with flux so the hard layer melts away
Grind it back to sound metal and check it for cracks
Weld the root at a higher current to melt the layer
questions.why: Thermal cutting hardens and oxidises the cut face of Cr-Mo, and without preheat it can crack. The procedure is to preheat before cutting; if that was missed, grind back to sound, bright metal and check by MT or PT.

questions.q: A welder accidentally strikes an arc on a P11 pipe 30 mm from the groove. What is the usual remedy?
o: Weld a small bead over it to hide the burn mark
Leave it, because PWHT will soften the spot
Paint over it so it does not rust in service
Grind it out smoothly and check it by MT or PT
questions.why: An arc strike on Cr-Mo leaves a hard spot that can crack. It is reported, ground out smoothly and checked by MT or PT (and hardness if the procedure asks), then recorded.

questions.q: Why does the WPS for P11 set a maximum interpass temperature as well as a minimum preheat?
o: To save fuel gas on the heating torch
Too much heat lowers the toughness of the weld and HAZ
So that the electrodes in the quiver do not overheat
So that the pipe does not get too hot for the welder's gloves
questions.why: Building up too much heat coarsens the grain and spoils the toughness and strength of the weld and HAZ. The WPS range keeps the joint warm enough to stop cracking, but not so hot that the metal is harmed.
